Equivariant Diffusion Policy.narr: Ordinary behavior cloning wastes demonstrations: showing a robot how to grasp a mug at one angle teaches it almost nothing about grasping it rotated 30°. The fix is to bake in the geometry itself — guarantee SO(2) rotational symmetry at the network level so one demo automatically teaches every rotated version.
Equivariant Diffusion Policy.how:
Build the symmetry rule into the architecture: use rotation-equivariant convolutions or feature transforms so the network is guaranteed to rotate actions whenever the input rotates, rather than learning it from scratch.

The machine: when the image rotates by angle θ, the network's outputs rotate by θ as well, by design. Train once on a few rotations and the policy generalizes to all of them for free.

Result: 21.9% higher success on 6-DoF control using far fewer demonstrations — the same hours of video teach an order of magnitude more poses.

ALOHA Unleashed.narr: Imitation learning on contact-rich, deformable tasks (bimanual folding, cloth, soft objects) breaks because actions in narrow contact regimes don't average — a grasp that works for fabric fails if you average it with another valid grasp. Scaling diffusion to bimanual, high-dimensional action spaces keeps all the modes alive.
ALOHA Unleashed.how:
1. Collect large-scale demonstrations from teleoperated bimanual arms across deformable and contact-rich tasks (ALOHA dataset, 50k+ trajectories).
  2. Train a diffusion policy conditioned on dual wrist cameras and proprioception to generate high-dimensional bimanual action chunks.
  3. At test time, denoise from noise into coordinated bimanual actions that preserve contact and fold geometry.

Denoising handles the discontinuous contact dynamics and multimodal contact configurations that regression-based BC collapses.

3D Diffusion Policy (DP3).narr: A policy trained on raw pixel observations breaks catastrophically when the camera shifts — the scene looks completely different even though the task geometry hasn't changed. The fix is to condition on compact 3D point-cloud representations instead of pixels, making the policy reliable to viewpoint while keeping sample efficiency high.
3D Diffusion Policy (DP3).how:
1. Lift observations into 3D: use a SLAM or depth backbone to build a point cloud from the camera frame.
  2. Feed compact 3D tokens into the denoiser, which generates actions or pose trajectories in 3D space.
  3. Because the policy reasons geometrically, it holds up under camera motion, lighting changes, and new object instances in the same spatial layout.

Viewpoint-reliability emerges from 3D reasoning alone, not learned invariance — so 40 demos suffice where pixel-based methods need hundreds.

GenDP.narr: Vision-only policies hit a ceiling on unseen-object generalization (around 20% success) because they never see the specific object at test time, only spatially-similar stand-ins. Adding semantic 3D fields that embed object category and geometry lets the policy recognize 'a mug is a mug' and reuse the grasp across unseen instances.
GenDP.how:
1. Extract semantic 3D fields from the scene — per-voxel embeddings that encode object category, part labels, and material.
  2. Condition the denoiser on both the visual observation and the semantic field.
  3. The diffusion process learns to query the semantic field to decide where and how to grasp, parameterized by object properties rather than pixel coordinates.

Generalization to unseen objects jumps from 20% to 93% because the policy learns a semantic grasp strategy, not a camera-frame lookup table.

Generative Image as Action Models.narr: Action distributions can be visualized but not directly trained: a diffusion head predicts noise in latent action space, making it opaque whether the policy has learned the right skill. A surprising fix is to fine-tune Stable Diffusion to draw actions as joint trajectories on the image itself, turning the policy into a visual interpreter.
Generative Image as Action Models.how:
1. Set up Stable Diffusion to generate images conditioned on the observation.
  2. Fine-tune the model so the generated image draws the joint trajectory — overlaid as curves over the robot's state.
  3. Sample the diffusion process to generate unseen trajectories, then extract the drawn action from the output image.

The action becomes interpretable (you can see it), multimodal (different samples draw different paths), and grounded in vision all at once, bridging generative models and visuomotor control.

From Imitation to Refinement.narr: Behavior cloning from demonstrations gives you a policy, but it only replicates what the data showed—it never fixes the mistakes the demonstrators made or adapts to new situations. This paper keeps the cloned base but freezes it, then adds a residual RL layer to refine the actions where the clone errs, correcting distribution shift between training and deployment without destabilizing the learned behavior.
From Imitation to Refinement.how:
The mechanism: train a diffusion policy to clone the demonstrations (the chunked trajectory baseline), then freeze those weights. On top, learn a small correction network via RL (typically PPO with a learned reward or human preference signal) that generates delta-actions to adjust the cloned trajectory. The residual stays bounded by KL-divergence regularization so the policy doesn't drift far from the cloned prior, maintaining stability.

Why it works: the clone already captures the demonstration distribution; RL tunes it toward better-than-demonstrations behavior while the KL regularization keeps it from collapsing into a different mode. The denoising trajectory gives RL a smooth, multimodal prior to refine rather than starting from scratch.

Streaming Diffusion Policy.narr: Denoising actions takes ~50 network passes, too slow for a control loop that needs a decision every 10 ms. This paper rolls partially-denoised futures forward as the robot executes, so the next chunk is ready before the current one finishes, amortizing the inference cost across multiple control steps instead of stalling between decisions.
Streaming Diffusion Policy.how:
The mechanism: predict a chunk of H future actions (H ≈ 8). As the robot executes the first k actions, continue the denoising of the remaining H-k steps in parallel. When k steps expire, the remaining chunk is already half-denoised; roll the partially-denoised states forward to account for elapsed time, then finish denoising. By pipelining, the wall-clock time between decisions shrinks from ~50 NFEs to ~10-15.

Why it works: partial denoising preserves the multimodal distribution (you're not committing to a final action yet), and rolling the trajectory forward is a cheap linear operation. The robot moves continuously without waiting for fresh plans to finish.

Real-time Iteration Scheme for Diffusion.narr: Control systems solve the next step by warm-starting from the previous solution—iteratively refining a trajectory at every tick. This paper applies the same idea to diffusion: instead of starting each denoising from pure noise, warm-start from the previous timestep's solution, taking only 3-5 denoising steps per cycle rather than 50, landing naturally into real-time control loops.
Real-time Iteration Scheme for Diffusion.how:
The mechanism: at control tick t, take the denoised action chunk from tick t-1, shift it one step forward (roll the trajectory), add a small amount of noise back (re-diffusion), then denoise for only 3-5 steps. This mimics classical iterative control: the solution at t-1 is already close to the optimal t; a few refinement steps land there. Because the prior is warm, few steps suffice.

Why it works: diffusion's denoising preserves the local structure of the trajectory. Warm-starting from a nearby solution lets you skip the first 40-45 noisy steps and go straight to refinement. Each cycle completes in milliseconds, feeding a fast control loop while staying multimodal.

RA-DP.narr: Most diffusion policies denoise once, offline, then execute; they can't react to unexpected obstacles or disturbances mid-trajectory. RA-DP injects guidance at every denoising step to steer the action away from hazards on the fly—no retraining, no rerolling the entire action, just nudging what's already being denoised in real time.
RA-DP.how:
The mechanism: run denoising as normal, but at each of the K steps, compute a cost gradient (distance to obstacle, collision likelihood, constraint violation) and push the denoising trajectory in the direction that lowers that cost. The gradient is injected into the prediction-correction loop; each denoised intermediate state bends away from the hazard slightly.

Why it works: because denoising is iterative, the trajectory hasn't committed to a risky action yet. Steering one step at a time integrates into a globally safer path. No retraining needed: the same frozen policy responds to new costs by changing the denoising trajectory on-the-fly.

3D Diffuser Actor.narr: Policies that condition on 2D pixels fail the moment the camera moves or lighting shifts—the pixel distribution changes while the right action hasn't. This paper lifts observations into 3D (point clouds) and conditions a 3D denoising transformer on that geometry, predicting 3D end-effector poses directly, making the policy handle viewpoint and lighting variation while staying sample-efficient.
3D Diffuser Actor.how:
The mechanism: encode the point cloud into a 3D scene representation (e.g., tokens per spatial region or voxel); use a transformer to fuse the cloud with the task observation (goal, language, proprioception). The denoiser conditions on that 3D representation via cross-attention and predicts a 3D trajectory (end-effector positions and orientations). Denoising happens in 3D space, not pixel space.

Why it works: 3D geometry is viewpoint-invariant. The same point cloud under a different camera angle represents the same scene, so the learned denoising generalizes. Predicting in 3D naturally produces spatially coherent trajectories, and the policy sees far fewer irrelevant pixels—only the relevant 3D structure.

PointFlowMatch.narr: Consistency models and flow matching speed up denoising by 10-50×; this paper combines flow matching with point-cloud conditioning to get both speed and 3D invariance. Flow matching on point clouds learns a velocity field in 3D space you can integrate in 1-2 steps, hitting 67.8% on RLBench—2× the next-best—while staying viewpoint-agnostic.
PointFlowMatch.how:
The mechanism: condition on the point cloud representation; learn a velocity field v(x, t, obs) that points from random initial actions toward good actions. Given a noise sample, integrate the ODE dx/dt = v(x, t, obs) for a few steps (1-2 typically). The velocity is trained by comparing trajectories sampled at different times and matching the flow. No intermediate denoising steps needed; one integration solves.

Why it works: the velocity field is smoother than iterative denoising, so integration converges fast. Point-cloud conditioning keeps it geometrically grounded. The flow learns the entire distribution implicitly in the vector field, so sampling is as simple as following one smooth curve from noise to action.

DiffuView.narr: Learning 3D-invariant action features from scratch requires heavy 3D annotation. This paper pre-trains a diffusion model on multi-view image sets, forcing the encoder to build 3D-consistent latent features that don't change when the viewpoint shifts. Fine-tuning on real manipulation then uses those invariant features, achieving 92.2% LIBERO with far fewer task-specific demos.
DiffuView.how:
The mechanism: in pretraining, show the model multiple views of the same scene and the same action trajectory. Denoise action from each view independently. Loss: the denoised actions must be consistent despite different camera angles (penalize differences between views). The encoder learns to extract invariant 3D structure from 2D pixels. At task time, the learned encoder feeds into a task-specific policy head.

Why it works: multi-view consistency is a strong self-supervised signal for 3D structure. By forcing the encoder to ignore view changes, it learns geometry, not appearance. Tasks then inherit that invariance; new viewpoints generalize because the features already encode the 3D layout.

Render and Diffuse.narr: Policies struggle when the robot goes out of frame or the camera angle changes mid-task. This paper explicitly renders the robot's predicted pose into the image—overlaying where the end-effector will be—then denoises the render to refine both the pose and the action, grounding predictions in spatial image reasoning for better generalization.
Render and Diffuse.how:
The mechanism: predict a noisy end-effector pose; render it into the camera image as a 3D overlay (silhouette, skeleton, or texture). Condition the denoiser on both the observation and the rendered prediction. Denoise jointly over pose and pixel space so the network sees the predicted action visualized on the scene. Loss includes both pose accuracy and render-observation consistency.

Why it works: rendering makes spatial relationships explicit and visual. The denoiser sees the pose prediction in context, so it can correct occlusions and camera variations by reasoning about the image directly. Tying denoising to the render ties the learned policy to the coordinate system that matters for execution.

EquiBot.narr: A single demonstration of grasping a mug teaches almost nothing about grasping the same mug rotated 30°—demonstrations are expensive. EquiBot hard-codes SIM(3)-equivariance (scale, rotation, translation invariance) into the denoiser, so one demo automatically teaches every transformed version, dramatically cutting sample complexity for 6-DoF manipulation.
EquiBot.how:
The mechanism: use equivariant neural networks (e.g., those respecting SO(3) on orientation and translation groups). Structure the denoiser so that rotating the observation rotates the predicted action by the same amount. This is not learned; it's baked into the architecture—e.g., via group convolutions or Lie-algebra reparameterization. The policy then provably generalizes to unseen rotations and scales.

Why it works: manipulation is fundamentally equivariant—rotate the scene and the right move rotates identically. Hard-coding this constraint means one demo covers the entire rotation and scale space. Data efficiency jumps because generalization is geometric, not learned.

Consistency Policy.narr: Diffusion's speed problem is real: 50+ denoising passes per action is too slow for mobile or resource-constrained robots. Consistency models distill the many-step process into a single jump from noise to clean action—consistency distillation—delivering 10× faster inference while keeping the multimodal expressiveness, enabling deployment on edge hardware.
Consistency Policy.how:
The mechanism: train a consistency function f(x, t) that maps from any noisy action at any diffusion timestep t directly to the clean action. Distill by running a teacher diffusion model on many trajectories; for each noisy intermediate state, the consistency function should predict the final action. The loss penalizes mismatch: L = ||f(x_t, t) - f(x_s, s)||, enforcing that all intermediate states point to the same clean output.

Why it works: once trained, f skips iterative refinement and produces a clean action in one pass. The multimodal structure is implicit in f's learned parameterization (f can produce different outputs for similar noisy inputs if the teacher distribution is bimodal). One-step inference replaces 50 steps, fitting inside real-time loops on CPU/mobile.

WAM-Flow.narr: Trajectory planning for autonomous driving needs multimodal predictions (turn left, straight, right) and high throughput (>10 Hz). Discrete flow matching over trajectory tokens generates diverse driving plans directly from a latent vocabulary without iterative sampling, achieving 3× speedup while maintaining multimodal expressiveness.
WAM-Flow.how:
The problem: Diffusion-based motion planning for driving is accurate but slow; iterative DDPM sampling takes dozens of steps. Multimodal predictions require either expensive per-mode sampling or lossy discretization; classical planners lose the ability to sample diverse-but-valid alternatives.

The mechanism: Tokenize trajectories as a sequence of discrete waypoint tokens (e.g., 2D positions quantized to a codebook). Train a flow-matching model over this discrete space, conditioned on the ego vehicle's state and the scene context. At inference, sample different trajectory tokens in sequence using integrated flow (1–3 steps), pulling from different regions of the latent space to get diverse driving plans.

Why it works: Discrete flow matching skips iterative sampling; integrating the flow field for one or a few steps gives a complete trajectory token sequence. Sampling from different latent regions naturally generates diverse plans without per-mode overhead. 3× speedup + multimodality makes this deployable in real-time autonomous stacks.

MeanFuser.narr: Predicting the next few seconds of pedestrian or vehicle motion for autonomous planning is multimodal — they might turn left, go straight, or accelerate — and a single averaged prediction is dangerously wrong. One-step multimodal generation using discrete flow matching samples several distinct futures in a single forward pass at real-time speed, giving planners the full distribution they need.
MeanFuser.how:
The problem: A car or pedestrian can move in several valid ways (turn left or right at an intersection); a regressor outputs the mean path, which often passes through the middle (where no one actually goes). Sampling diverse futures at 59 FPS is too slow for real-time autonomous driving.

The mechanism: Encode motion as discrete trajectory tokens (e.g., quantized waypoints in a latent space). Train a flow-matching model over this discrete space conditioned on the agent's past trajectory and scene context. At inference, sample multiple distinct trajectories in parallel by drawing different flow paths through the latent space. Each sample takes one step thanks to flow matching's direct integration.

Why it works: Discrete flow matching avoids expensive iterative refinement; one forward pass generates a trajectory. Sampling multiple trajectories in parallel gives the planner a multimodal distribution without the latency of DDPM-style sequential sampling. 59 FPS throughput makes it deployable in autonomous-driving stacks.

SemanticVLA.narr: A language instruction like 'put the mug on the shelf' is inherently loose: the same phrase could mean many valid positions, angles, and gripper widths. Naive policies either output one averaged action that satisfies no particular interpretation, or they struggle to stay reliable when the phrasing changes. SemanticVLA solves this by having the model first reason out explicit spatial waypoints (intermediate poses the arm should visit) before diffusing the full action sequence, so one language instruction maps to a tight cluster of valid motor commands. The policy learns to parse language into geometry, then turn that geometry into executable actions.
SemanticVLA.how:
The problem: map instruction → action while respecting multimodality and language variance.

  1. Encode the language instruction and camera image into a shared embedding space.
  2. A planning head outputs explicit waypoint tokens — discrete spatial landmarks that anchor the task (e.g., 'grasp position', 'place position', 'clearance height').
  3. Encode those waypoints as latent action tokens alongside the image and language.
  4. A diffusion decoder denoises the full action sequence, conditioned on all three: language, image, and waypoint latents.
  5. The waypoints constrain the sampling, so rephrased instructions that map to the same geometry generate similar actions.

ACoT-VLA.narr: Long, multi-step manipulation tasks (assemble-and-place) defeat single-step policies because each action must commit to a longer chain of reasoning that the policy has no time to do. ACoT-VLA breaks this bind by first having the model decompose the task into a chain-of-thought sequence of intermediate actions — a verbal plan of what to do step by step — and only then predicting the actual motor commands conditioned on that reasoning. Language reasoning becomes the bridge between instruction and action.
ACoT-VLA.how:
The machinery separates reasoning from execution.

  1. Given a complex instruction (text + image), an LLM head generates a sequence of sub-action descriptions: 'first move to the target object', 'grasp it', 'move to the destination', etc. — the chain of thought.
  2. These descriptions are encoded into context embeddings.
  3. A diffusion policy denoises the full action trajectory, conditioned on both the image and the chain-of-thought embeddings.
  4. Because the intermediate steps are explicit, the denoiser can allocate action budget to each sub-task coherently.
  5. The same instruction parsed into the same sub-steps generates consistent multimodal actions, even though the instruction phrasing varies.

Multimodal Diffusion Transformer.narr: Imposing language labels on every demonstration is expensive, and many robot datasets have unlabeled video. The Multimodal Diffusion Transformer sidesteps this by using only the goal state (a target image or description) rather than step-by-step language, and trains a single diffusion transformer that can handle both vision and language conditions interchangeably. With less than 2% of the training data labeled, it learns to condition on latent goal representations that the unlabeled data can still inform, achieving strong results on long-horizon tasks.
Multimodal Diffusion Transformer.how:
The system draws on unlabeled trajectory data by learning a shared latent goal space.

  1. Encode both language goals and visual goal states (target images) into a unified latent space.
  2. Train a transformer diffusion model over action sequences, where each step is conditioned on the current observation, the latent goal embedding, and a timestep indicator.
  3. The latent goal space is learned from both labeled (language) and unlabeled (vision-only) trajectories, so the model infers the goal intent from visual context alone when text is unavailable.
  4. At inference, specify a goal as either text or image; the model maps it to the shared space and denoises the action trajectory toward it.
  5. Sparse language labels guide the latent space, but visual consistency in unlabeled rollouts ensures generalization even with <2% annotations.

RACER.narr: A learned diffusion policy can make mistakes, and when it does, neither the human nor the system has a graceful way to recover — it just crashes or fails. RACER pairs a diffusion actor with a vision-language model supervisor that watches the execution and, if it detects failure or ambiguity, issues a recovery instruction in natural language. The actor then conditions its next denoised action on that linguistic recovery cue, steering around the error without retraining. Language becomes a real-time correction mechanism built into the loop.
RACER.how:
The system interleaves high-level reasoning with low-level action sampling.

  1. At each timestep, execute an action from the diffusion policy's sample, conditioned on the current image and any prior language instruction.
  2. A VLM supervisor observes the resulting state and the original goal, and generates a recovery instruction if something is awry: 'try grasping from the left' or 'avoid the obstacle'.
  3. That recovery text is encoded alongside the image into the diffusion policy's conditioning.
  4. The next denoising pass samples an action that respects both the goal and the recovery guidance.
  5. If the supervisor detects success, no instruction is issued, and the policy continues under the original goal alone.

Diffusion Meets Options.narr: A single flat diffusion policy cannot reliably plan coherent 100-step sequences; errors compound and it loses the high-level thread. Diffusion Meets Options applies the age-old control idea of options (temporally-extended actions) to diffusion: a high-level planner writes an LTL (linear temporal logic) formula that breaks a long task into subgoals, and for each subgoal interval, a low-level diffusion policy generates the trajectory to achieve it. Composability and reusability emerge from the decomposition.
Diffusion Meets Options.how:
Hierarchical planning decomposes long tasks into diffusion-sized chunks.

  1. A high-level planner interprets an LTL task specification (e.g., 'visit region A, then region B') and decomposes it into a sequence of subgoals and time horizons.
  2. For each (subgoal, horizon) pair, a diffusion trajectory generator denoises a segment of actions that steer the robot from its current state toward the subgoal within that horizon.
  3. Execute the first few actions of that segment, then replan from the achieved state to the next subgoal.
  4. Because subgoals are discrete and reusable, the same policy segments compose into unseen long-horizon tasks.
  5. Errors in one segment do not cascade; replanning at the next subgoal boundary provides a correction opportunity.

Diffusion Forcing Planner.narr: Trajectory prediction for autonomous vehicles is hard because the future is long and multimodal (many valid paths through the same scene), yet most planners collapse it into one averaged prediction. Diffusion Forcing Planner generates whole trajectory sequences per segment with per-segment noise initialization and history-annealed guidance, so each temporal chunk conditions on the vehicle's past while the denoiser respects hard constraints (lane bounds, collision-free). One model handles both prediction and planning.
Diffusion Forcing Planner.how:
The machinery breaks long trajectories into manageable diffusion segments.

  1. Initialize a trajectory chunk by sampling noise, but condition the noise on the history of observed states so the chunk begins believably from where the vehicle ended.
  2. At each denoising step, nudge the trajectory away from obstacles and out-of-lane regions using a guidance gradient (classifier-free or learned cost).
  3. Gradually anneal (reduce) the history conditioning strength as you denoise, transitioning from 'follow prior motion' to 'optimize for the goal'.
  4. Generate each segment's trajectory by denoising under these annealed constraints.
  5. Chain segments together with warm-started initialization (use the tail of one segment as the seed for the next) to maintain temporal coherence.

MetaFold.narr: Garment folding across different clothing categories is a prototypical deformable-object manipulation task where the same gripper motion on a shirt is wrong for a towel. Naive policies overfit to one category or mush all categories together into a useless average. MetaFold learns a language-guided point-cloud trajectory generator: the model ingests the category name in language and a point cloud of the garment, and denoises a 3D end-effector trajectory that respects the deformable physics of that specific garment type. Generalization comes from conditioning on both the language category prior and the observed point cloud geometry.
MetaFold.how:
The system generates category-aware 3D manipulation by fusing language and geometry.

  1. Encode the garment type as a language embedding ('shirt', 'towel', 'jacket') and the unfolded garment's point cloud into a unified representation.
  2. A diffusion model denoises a sequence of 3D end-effector poses, conditioned on both the language category and the point-cloud geometry.
  3. The point cloud and language together constrain the denoised trajectory — the trajectory must work for that specific garment and shape, not a generic cloth.
  4. Execute the denoised trajectory with a motion controller.
  5. Because language and point clouds co-condition the diffusion, the same model transfers to unseen garments and folds of the same category without retraining.

Goal-Reaching from Non-Expert Observatio.narr: Robots need subgoal sequences to chain long tasks, but annotating intermediate subgoals by hand is expensive and brittle. This work trains a diffusion policy as a high-level planner that watches a non-expert demonstration video and generates waypoint subgoals that a low-level controller can then execute. The high-level policy learns to decompose messy, inefficient human motion into a clean sequence of reachable waypoints, bridging the gap between unstructured observation and structured control.
Goal-Reaching from Non-Expert Observatio.how:
A diffusion model learns to infer subgoals from raw observations.

  1. Given a video of non-expert behavior (raw human reaching motions), encode the start frame and goal frame, plus intermediate observation frames, into latent representations.
  2. A diffusion policy denoises a sequence of intermediate subgoal poses — poses that, if executed, would trace a path from start to goal that respects the low-level controller's capabilities.
  3. The diffusion model is trained on pairs of non-expert trajectories and optimal subgoal sequences, learning to infer the subgoal structure from observation noise.
  4. At test time, condition on the start, goal, and any intermediate frames, and sample subgoals.
  5. Pass those subgoals to a low-level controller which executes each one in sequence, achieving the long-horizon task with a cleaner path than the original demo.

CrossFormer.narr: Every robot is morphologically different — an arm, a quadruped, a humanoid, a drone — so the field has built separate policies for each, wasting data and never letting one robot learn from another. CrossFormer breaks this by training one diffusion policy over 20 different embodiments simultaneously: the model sees demonstrations from all morphologies and learns a morphology-agnostic representation of observations and actions so the same weights can drive any body. A generalist policy matches specialists trained on each body alone.
CrossFormer.how:
The machinery abstracts away morphology through a shared latent space.

  1. For each morphology (arm, quadruped, humanoid, etc.), encode its proprioceptive state (joint angles, velocities) into a shared latent space using morphology-specific encoders.
  2. Similarly encode camera observations and goal specifications into the same space.
  3. Train a single diffusion policy over this shared space, learning to denoise action trajectories that any morphology can decode back into its own joint commands.
  4. Each morphology has its own decoder that maps shared latent actions back to joint torques or velocities.
  5. Because the shared space is learned jointly over all morphologies, demonstration diversity across embodiments helps the policy generalize, and a new morphology needs far less data to adapt.

One Policy to Run Them All.narr: The hypothesis behind this work is that morphology should not matter if observations and actions are encoded smartly. One Policy to Run Them All trains a diffusion policy using morphology-agnostic encoders — encoders that produce the same latent representation for the same task regardless of the body executing it — achieving zero-shot transfer across quadrupeds, humanoids, hexapods, and even wheeled robots. The policy itself becomes a universal bridge between any observational modality and any action space.
One Policy to Run Them All.how:
The key is learning invariant representations of task structure.

  1. Design observation encoders that extract task-relevant features (e.g., 'target position relative to gripper' or 'terrain slope') in a body-agnostic way.
  2. Learn shared goal representations: a goal image or language description produces the same embedding regardless of which robot processes it.
  3. Train the diffusion policy on this shared goal and observation embedding alongside morphology-specific action decoders.
  4. At test time, encode the observation and goal in the universal space, run diffusion, and decode the action for the target morphology.
  5. Because the observation and goal encodings are invariant, a policy trained on quadrupeds can steer humanoids without retraining — the decoder handles the morphology gap.

Octo.narr: Most manipulation policies are closed-source and task-specific, trained on proprietary robotics data. Octo is an open-source generalist policy trained on a diverse public dataset of robot demonstrations across many tasks and embodiments. It uses a diffusion action head that samples multimodal actions conditioned on vision and language, making it sample-efficient and generalizable. It captures the state of the field: a public model you can run, finetune, or analyze.
Octo.how:
The machinery combines a visual foundation model with diffusion sampling.

  1. Encode camera images and goal descriptions using pretrained vision-language model components.
  2. Condition a diffusion policy head on those encodings, learning to denoise action trajectories.
  3. The diffusion head naturally captures action multimodality: given the same observation, multiple valid actions are possible (grasp left or right, approach slow or fast), and sampling from the diffusion model explores that distribution.
  4. Train on a diverse public dataset of demonstrations (BRIDGE, DROID, etc.) to build a generalist prior.
  5. Users can finetune on their own data or run it zero-shot; the model ships with checkpoints trained on hundreds of thousands of episodes.

PoCo.narr: Real robots have many sensory streams — cameras, depth sensors, proprioception, tactile feedback — and most policies lock into a single modality or fuse them in ad-hoc ways. PoCo treats multimodal inputs and outputs as a composition problem: each modality gets its own diffusion encoder and decoder, and a central policy learns to orchestrate all of them. Tactile and vision inform the plan; proprioception and force commands execute it. One system, many modalities and domains.
PoCo.how:
Modular diffusion encoders and decoders enable composition.

  1. For each input modality (camera, depth, tactile, proprioceptor), train or load an encoder that produces a latent feature vector.
  2. Concatenate (or sum with learned weights) all modal latents into a single context vector.
  3. A diffusion policy denoises an action sequence conditioned on this multimodal context.
  4. The predicted action latents pass through separate decoders: one outputs joint torques, another outputs gripper force, another outputs a tactile exploration target.
  5. Because each modality has its own encoder and decoder, swapping modalities or adding new ones requires only training new encoders/decoders, not retraining the core policy.

DiffusionSeeder.narr: Classical motion planners are slow (take seconds to find a path), and sampling-based planners like RRT converge slowly in cluttered spaces. DiffusionSeeder flips the problem: use a diffusion model to generate a batch of collision-free trajectory samples in milliseconds, then feed those samples as warm-start seeds to a fast GPU-based trajectory optimizer. Diffusion provides the creativity (many diverse routes), and the optimizer polishes them. Result: 12× average and 36× worst-case speedup over sampling planners.
DiffusionSeeder.how:
The machinery chains generative sampling with classical optimization.

  1. Condition a diffusion trajectory generator on start position, goal position, and a point cloud or occupancy map of the scene.
  2. Denoise several whole trajectories in parallel, each representing a different route through the obstacles.
  3. Pass the denoised trajectories as initial guesses (warm starts) to a GPU motion optimizer that refines them under collision and smoothness constraints.
  4. The optimizer converges faster because it begins near a good solution instead of from random initialization.
  5. Return the best-optimized trajectory, or multiple trajectories ranked by optimality metrics (length, clearance) to downstream planners.

Joint Localization and Planning Using Di.narr: Mobile robots need to know where they are and where they're going, but global localization (figuring out initial position in a known map) and path planning are usually solved separately with different algorithms. This work unifies both into one diffusion model: given a LiDAR scan and a goal location, a single denoiser produces both the robot's current SE(2) pose and the collision-free path to the goal. Jointly optimizing avoids brittleness and lets the two tasks inform each other.
Joint Localization and Planning Using Di.how:
A single diffusion model solves two coupled geometric problems.

  1. Encode the LiDAR scan as a point cloud and the goal location as a latent vector.
  2. Denoise a combined output: the robot's pose (x, y, θ) and a path trajectory to the goal.
  3. Train on pairs of (LiDAR, true pose, goal, optimal path) by predicting noise added during training.
  4. At inference, sample a pose and path jointly: the denoiser learns that certain poses make certain paths valid (must align with map structure).
  5. This joint inference often recovers from localization ambiguity faster than sequential solve because bad pose guesses make implausible paths, providing error signal.

GuideFlow.narr: Autonomous driving planners must obey hard constraints (stay in lane, don't hit pedestrians), but diffusion and flow-matching models are naturally soft optimizers that trade off objectives. GuideFlow embeds hard constraints directly into the velocity field of a flow-matching model: the model learns a velocity vector field that point trajectories are attracted to, and that field is sculpted to route around obstacles and respect lane boundaries by design, not as a soft penalty. Hard constraints become structural.
GuideFlow.how:
The machinery bakes constraints into the learned flow field.

  1. Define a constraint cost function: distance to lane boundary, distance to obstacles, etc.
  2. Train a flow-matching model to learn a velocity field vθ(x, t) that denoises trajectories.
  3. Apply constraint guidance during training: nudge the velocity field to decrease constraint cost at each point.
  4. At inference, integrate the learned velocity field: sample an initial trajectory from Gaussian noise and follow the field for a few steps, naturally routing toward high-probability and low-cost regions.
  5. The field structure ensures hard constraints are rarely violated; the model learns to satisfy them as part of the flow geometry rather than as post-hoc corrections.

Aerobatic Flight via Diffusion.narr: Flying aggressive maneuvers (barrel rolls, tight loops) is a distribution far from 'staying stable' in any normal dataset, yet diffusion policies can learn aerobatic primitives from trajectory data and explore that multimodal distribution safely. Aerobatic Flight via Diffusion trains a policy on aerobatic rollouts and uses classifier-guided batch sampling to avoid obstacles while maintaining the aerobatic character of the motion. Aggressive motion and safety constraints coexist in one diffusion model.
Aerobatic Flight via Diffusion.how:
The system balances learned primitive dynamics with safety guidance.

  1. Collect or simulate a dataset of aerobatic maneuvers (rolls, loops, spins).
  2. Train a diffusion policy to denoise action sequences that match the aerobatic distribution.
  3. At inference, condition the denoiser on the current state and apply a learned classifier guidance that scores trajectories by collision cost.
  4. At each denoising step, nudge the sample away from predicted collisions while keeping it aerobatic (don't let guidance pull it into stable, boring motion).
  5. Sample a batch of trajectories under this guidance and execute the best one — you get aerial acrobatics that avoid obstacles.

Potential Field-Guided Flow Matching.narr: Obstacle avoidance in learned policies is tricky: you can't retrain for every new environment. Potential Field-Guided Flow Matching applies a classical robotics idea (potential fields) to modern flow-matching sampling: the policy learns a base flow model over safe demonstrations, then at inference, a potential field gradient steers the flow away from obstacles while keeping the action valid and on-task. One learned policy handles many obstacle configurations without retraining.
Potential Field-Guided Flow Matching.how:
Guidance gradients sculpt the learned flow toward safety.

  1. Train a flow-matching model on demonstrations with the goal of learning the distribution of good actions.
  2. At inference, compute a potential field from the observed obstacles: a scalar cost function that increases near obstacles.
  3. Compute the gradient of this potential with respect to the action trajectory — the direction that decreases collision cost.
  4. At each flow integration step, nudge the trajectory by a weighted sum of the flow direction and the potential gradient.
  5. The flow provides task knowledge (what actions work for the task) and the potential field provides safety (what trajectories avoid collisions), so the result is safe, on-task behavior even in new scenes.

Physics-Informed Conditional Diffusion (.narr: Vehicle dynamics change dramatically with tire and road conditions (wet asphalt vs. snow), but naive policies trained in one condition fail catastrophically in others. Physics-Informed Conditional Diffusion learns a diffusion policy for drifting and other high-traction maneuvers, then at inference, adapts the diffusion conditioner with physics priors: given an estimate of current friction, road angle, and load, the model reconditions the policy to generate actions that respect that physics. One policy adapts to many tire/road pairs without retraining.
Physics-Informed Conditional Diffusion (.how:
Physics parameters inform conditioning without retraining.

  1. Train a diffusion policy on drifting maneuvers with multimodal conditions: image, state, and a latent intent (slow drift, aggressive drift).
  2. Estimate the current environmental physics: tire-road friction coefficient, road grade, vehicle load (from sensor fusion or telemetry).
  3. Pass these physics parameters as additional conditional inputs to the denoiser during sampling.
  4. The denoiser learns which action samples are consistent with those physics (high friction allows tighter, faster drifts; low friction requires wider turns).
  5. At each denoising step, the action gets updated toward a trajectory that respects both the learned policy and the current physics, so the same weights adapt to snow, dry asphalt, or ice.

Risk-Averse Diffusion Policies.narr: Offline reinforcement learning is risky: the policy might sample actions far outside the training distribution and crash. Risk-Averse Diffusion Policies augments a diffusion policy with a distributional perspective: instead of predicting one action, the model predicts a whole distribution of action outcomes and their risks. Then it uses risk-averse optimization to pick actions that maximize expected reward while staying conservative about uncertainty. You get better offline RL without more data.
Risk-Averse Diffusion Policies.how:
The machinery trades off reward against distributional uncertainty.

  1. Train a diffusion model to denoise action sequences, and alongside it, learn a critic that predicts the return (cumulative reward) and its variance for each action.
  2. At inference, sample a batch of denoised actions.
  3. Score each action using a risk-averse objective: mean return minus a scaled variance penalty (CVaR or worst-case-weighted return).
  4. Select the action that maximizes this risk-averse score, biasing toward actions with high reward and low uncertainty.
  5. This penalizes out-of-distribution actions more heavily (they have high variance) so the offline policy stays conservative while still improving on the demos.

NaviDiffuser.narr: Real navigation involves trading off multiple objectives in real time: get to the goal, but avoid obstacles, respect energy limits, and stay comfortable for passengers. Retraining a policy for every trade-off is wasteful. NaviDiffuser learns one diffusion policy and enables real-time multi-objective control using weight-range guidance: at inference, specify a range of weights for each objective (safety 0.1–0.9, speed 0.2–0.8, comfort 0.3–0.7), and the sampler explores trajectories that balance within those ranges. One policy becomes a family of behaviors tuned on the fly.
NaviDiffuser.how:
Flexible guidance weights enable real-time multi-objective trade-offs.

  1. Train a diffusion policy on demonstrations with multiple outcome signals: safety score (inverse collision cost), speed, comfort (acceleration smoothness).
  2. At inference, encode each objective as a learned classifier or reward model that scores trajectories.
  3. During denoising, apply guidance from all objectives with user-specified weights: nudge toward high safety if safety weight is high, toward high speed if speed weight is high.
  4. Allow ranges for weights (not fixed values) so the sampler can adaptively balance within the specified bounds.
  5. The user dials safety vs. speed vs. comfort without retraining; the learned denoiser handles the orchestration.

3D-ViTac.narr: Manipulation by sight alone fails the moment fingers touch an object — the physics turns discontinuous and cameras often cannot see into tight grasps. Tactile sensing solves this: folding touch feedback into the denoiser gives fine force control for contact-rich tasks like pressing, sliding, and assembly where vision alone fumbles.
3D-ViTac.how:
The problem: Vision sees the scene but not what happens at the finger-object interface; when contact dynamics dominate (a fragile item, in-hand manipulation), the policy needs proprioceptive ground truth.

The mechanism: Collect both camera images and tactile readings (pressure, shear, vibration) into a unified 3D visuo-tactile representation. The denoiser conditions on both modalities jointly, learning a fused space where tactile signals inform contact forces and camera features guide reach direction.

Why it works: At contact, tactile feedback becomes the primary signal; the denoiser uses it to commit to a specific pressure profile or slip velocity instead of guessing from the image alone. On fragile and occluded tasks, touch + diffusion consistently outperforms vision-only.

Implicit Contact Diffuser.narr: Model-predictive control for manipulation gets stuck at local minima when trying to solve contact transitions — press then slide requires predicting a discontinuity and reversing a trajectory if wrong. Latent diffusion over contact descriptors lets the policy propose multiple candidate contact modes; MPC then refines the best one, sidestepping local traps.
Implicit Contact Diffuser.how:
The problem: Discontinuous contact dynamics (stick, slip, lift) create local minima that gradient-based optimizers can't escape; a single forward pass either guesses wrong or leaves the policy half-committed.

The mechanism: Train a latent diffusion model over contact state descriptors (friction cone angle, normal force, slip direction). At run time, sample a diverse set of contact trajectories from the diffusion prior, then initialize MPC from each one and solve for the full trajectory. Keep the solution with lowest cost.

Why it works: Diffusion provides a diverse set of plausible contact transitions, and MPC refines from a warm start. Instead of climbing out of a single local minimum, the hybrid explores multiple valleys in parallel.

ProDapt.narr: A robot hand can complete a task from tactile memory alone if it has learned to attend to long-term contact history — how the object shifted, whether it slipped, what corrective move came next. Long-term tactile memory lets a diffusion policy complete manipulation using only proprioception and touch, even if vision is occluded or the workspace is dark.
ProDapt.how:
The problem: Vision-based policies fail when the target object is occluded (in-hand) or the workspace is unlit; proprioception alone (joint angles, velocities) is too sparse to guide contact-rich manipulation.

The mechanism: Augment the diffusion denoiser with a rolling history of tactile observations — pressure maps, shear vectors, vibration spectra over the last T steps. At each denoising step, the policy conditions on this tactile history and proprioceptive state, learning to infer object geometry and friction from touch alone.

Why it works: Tactile memory encodes object-level information (shape, stiffness, slip direction) that proprioception cannot; the denoiser learns to read that signal across a sequence of touches and generate contact-consistent actions even in darkness or total occlusion.

PolyTouch.narr: Most tactile sensors are either camera-based (high bandwidth, fragile) or simple pressure arrays (reliable, coarse). Multi-modal tactile fusion — combining camera and acoustic sensing in a single learned representation — gives both richness and reliability for contact-rich policies, especially on deformable objects.
PolyTouch.how:
The problem: Single-modality tactile sensors are brittle: optical sensors saturate or break, pressure arrays are too coarse for dexterous control on deformable items like cloth.

The mechanism: Fuse camera-based tactile images and acoustic emissions (sound of slip, vibration on contact) into a joint 3D tactile descriptor. Feed both into the denoiser so it learns to weight each modality's signal based on task phase: acoustic dominates early (detecting slip), optical leads when tracking fine geometry later.

Why it works: Acoustic signals slip and stick events faster than pressure; optical captures texture and edges. The denoiser learns which sense to trust when, naturally blending modalities across the contact sequence. On soft and deformable tasks, this multi-modal reliability exceeds any single sensor.

DiffuseLoco.narr: Walking gaits are multimodal — trot, bound, walk — and regression-trained policies average them into an unstable stumble. Diffusion in the control loop samples a committed gait from offline demonstrations; because action chunking keeps sampled motions smooth and because flow matching now fits into real-time rates, deployed legged robots can move reliably for the first time.
DiffuseLoco.how:
The problem: A walking robot has several valid gaits (trot, bound, gallop); behavior cloning via MSE loss outputs the mean gait, which is typically unstable and sits between two modes. The control loop also runs at 100+ Hz, leaving no time for slow diffusion sampling.

The mechanism: Collect offline logs of legged locomotion capturing multiple gaits. Train a diffusion policy on action chunks (a short sequence of joint commands). At run time, use consistency or flow-matching distillation to sample an action chunk in 1–5 steps instead of dozens, fitting it into a control tick. Execute the first few commands, then replan the next chunk from the current state.

Why it works: Denoising captures the full distribution of valid gaits, so sampling commits to one coherent trot or bound instead of averaging into the invalid in-between. Real-time flow matching makes this feasible on modest hardware; receding-horizon replanning keeps the trajectory stable and reactive.

Preference-Aligned Diffusion Planner for.narr: Offline data captured in simulation with one terrain rarely transfers to hardware in a new environment. Preference refinement — collecting a few trials in the new setting and using human feedback to steer the diffusion prior toward locally-successful gaits — achieves zero-shot sim-to-real without a full retraining loop.
Preference-Aligned Diffusion Planner for.how:
The problem: Sim-to-real for legged robots fails because simulated friction, compliance, and motor response differ from hardware; retraining from scratch on hardware is expensive, and fine-tuning a large policy is unstable.

The mechanism: Train an offline diffusion planner on simulation data. At deployment, run a handful of trials on the real robot and ask a human to rank which gaits worked best. Use those preferences to guide the sampling: at each denoising step, nudge the action toward high-ranked trajectories using a learned preference reward.

Why it works: Preference guidance steers the existing diffusion prior toward local-environment gaits without retraining the full model. A few human annotations are enough to anchor the policy to the real hardware's friction and dynamics.

Transferable Latent-to-Latent Locomotion.narr: Each legged robot has different leg lengths, mass distribution, and actuator limits; retraining a diffusion policy for every robot is wasteful. Latent-space residual modules learn robot-specific corrections on top of a shared core policy, so one base model transfers to many morphologies with minimal adaptation.
Transferable Latent-to-Latent Locomotion.how:
The problem: A diffusion policy trained on one quadruped (e.g., A1) does not generalize to another (e.g., Spot) because the action space is morphology-specific; retraining per-robot is expensive and slow.

The mechanism: Train a base diffusion policy on a reference morphology. For each new robot, learn a lightweight latent-to-latent residual module: it takes the base policy's latent noise-state and outputs a morphology-specific correction to the action. This module is small and data-efficient, trained from just a few hours of the new robot's data.

Why it works: The base policy captures the gait distribution across dynamics; the residual module accounts for morphology-specific asymmetries (different leg lengths, actuator saturation). Together, they transfer across robots with far less data than retraining from scratch.

Causal Motion Diffusion Models.narr: Generating human motion from text or music typically requires looking ahead to the full prompt, which breaks streaming and introduces latency. Causal diffusion — conditioning on only the past and current frame — enables live generation with order-of-magnitude lower latency, crucial for real-time animation and telepresence.
Causal Motion Diffusion Models.how:
The problem: Standard diffusion samples the full sequence conditioned on the text prompt, requiring the entire input before generation starts; this incurs seconds of latency, making live motion capture-to-motion pipelines impossible.

The mechanism: Restrict the attention and conditioning in the denoiser to only past frames and the current frame. At each timestep, denoise the next frame's joint angles using only the history of past poses and current frame observation, not future context. Autoregressively generate frame-by-frame.

Why it works: Causal masking makes the model commit to low-latency predictions; each frame depends only on the past, so generation can stream in real time. The latency drops from seconds (sample full sequence) to tens of milliseconds (denoise one frame).

PAMotion.narr: Generated human motions often violate physical constraints — floating feet, unrealistic joint accelerations, impossible balance — making them unsuitable for animation or control. Physics-aware denoising losses integrate contact and acceleration constraints directly into the diffusion training, ensuring generated motions remain physically plausible.
PAMotion.how:
The problem: A diffusion model trained on reconstructed motion-capture trajectories can produce unrealistic motions: feet sliding, excessive joint acceleration, or balance violations that no human could achieve.

The mechanism: Add auxiliary losses during training that penalize physics violations: measure contact (foot-ground distance), measure acceleration norms, estimate balance stability from center-of-mass projection. At each diffusion step, backpropagate these physics losses alongside the standard noise-prediction loss.

Why it works: Physics losses act as a soft constraint, nudging the denoiser toward trajectories with valid contact and dynamics. The model learns to trade off data likelihood (matching the distribution of training motions) against physical plausibility, naturally favoring motions that satisfy both.

SceMoS.narr: Human motion in a cluttered scene depends on local geometry — doorways, furniture, obstacles — but generative models often ignore the scene context and produce motions that collide or look misaligned. Scene-aware tokens — per-frame heightmaps or occupancy encoding — let the denoiser condition on the 3D layout, generating motions that respect the scene's affordances.
SceMoS.how:
The problem: Text-to-motion models generate plausible motions in isolation but ignore the spatial environment; a motion that works in an empty space may collide with furniture or look spatially misaligned in the actual scene.

The mechanism: Preprocess the scene as a heightmap or voxel occupancy grid at each frame. Encode this as tokens and feed into the diffusion denoiser alongside the text prompt. A token planner layer attends to the scene tokens to predict trajectory key points; the full motion denoiser then conditions on these waypoints, ensuring the body path avoids obstacles and respects the scene layout.

Why it works: Scene conditioning anchors the motion to local geometry; the planner-level waypoints act as intermediate targets that keep the full motion coherent. The denoiser learns to generate motions compatible with both the text and the scene, naturally avoiding collisions.

Retrieval-Guided Diffusion Noise Optimiz.narr: Highly constrained motion synthesis — full-body IK, contact preservation, footstep timing — is hard to specify as text alone. Retrieval-augmented initialization finds similar motions in a database and uses them to seed the diffusion noise, narrowing the search space so the denoiser can refine toward a valid solution.
Retrieval-Guided Diffusion Noise Optimiz.how:
The problem: Text descriptions of constrained motions are ambiguous and loose; "stand on one leg" has infinite solutions, and pure diffusion samples widely instead of focusing on the valid subspace.

The mechanism: Given a text prompt and constraints (e.g., contact points, keyframe positions), retrieve the nearest-neighbor motions from a motion database using semantic similarity. Use the nearest-neighbor's noise trajectory (in the diffusion latent space) as the initialization instead of pure Gaussian noise. Then denoise, biasing the sampler toward the retrieved exemplar's subspace.

Why it works: Starting from an exemplar's noise state dramatically narrows the search space; the denoiser only needs to refine and adapt the retrieved motion to satisfy the text and constraints, rather than generating from scratch. This is especially powerful for highly constrained problems where the valid subspace is small.

Gaussian-Mixture Latent Flow.narr: Forecasting human motion in 3D is multimodal and ambiguous: the person might reach left or right, sit or stand. Gaussian-mixture latent flow — learning a mixture of velocity fields over different modes — captures multiple futures and assigns probability to each, so predictions encode true uncertainty rather than blurred averages.
Gaussian-Mixture Latent Flow.how:
The problem: A single regression-based motion predictor outputs point estimates (one averaged trajectory); when the true future is multimodal (two equally plausible reaching directions), the mean is often invalid. Even sampling-based models can undercount the number of distinct modes.

The mechanism: Represent the latent distribution as a Gaussian mixture: learn K component velocity fields, each parameterized by a flow model. At inference, sample which mixture component (mode), then integrate its corresponding velocity field for a few steps. Assign probabilities to each mode based on the mixture weights and the input history.

Why it works: Explicit mixture modeling ensures the model maintains multiple distinct modes; each one is a separate flow trajectory, so they don't blur together. The mixture weights give downstream planning direct access to mode likelihoods instead of requiring expensive resampling or filtering.

PoseD-Flow.narr: Completing occluded human poses (filling in missing joints when limbs are hidden) is a manifold problem — joint angles live on rotation groups, not Euclidean space. Guided flow on the rotation manifold respects the geometric constraints of joint angles, generating geometrically valid and physically plausible completions even from heavy occlusion.
PoseD-Flow.how:
The problem: Predicting missing joint angles as points in Euclidean space violates the manifold structure of rotations; the output can be physically impossible (joint angles outside valid ranges, kinematic inversions). Naive diffusion treats rotations as flat vectors.

The mechanism: Parameterize joint angles as rotations (6D, quaternion, or axis-angle). Design the flow-matching velocity field to operate on the Riemannian manifold of rotations, respecting geodesic distances and intrinsic geometry. Use guidance to steer the flow toward visible joints and away from occlusion.

Why it works: Manifold-aware velocity fields guarantee outputs stay in the valid rotation space; the flow naturally interpolates between poses along geodesics, not straight lines through Euclidean space. Guided sampling steers the manifold flow toward observed joints and plausible human poses, ensuring physical validity under heavy occlusion.

RehearseVLA.narr: A vision-language-action policy trained on demonstration data alone can only replicate what it saw; it never discovers a better strategy and inherits any inefficiencies in the demos. Physically-consistent world model post-training — imagine futures with a learned model, then use RL to refine the VLA toward better imagined outcomes — lets a policy improve past the demonstrations using just a handful of real trials.
RehearseVLA.how:
The problem: Behavior cloning from demonstrations caps out at demonstrator skill; the policy can never exceed or correct the demos' mistakes. RL fine-tuning on real data is expensive and often unstable for complex manipulation tasks.

The mechanism: Train a dynamics model on simulation or offline data to predict the next observation and reward given an action. Start with a VLA policy trained by imitation learning. For each batch, roll out trajectories in the learned world model, score them against a reward signal, and use safe RL (e.g., TRPO, PPO with KL regularization to the behavioral cloning prior) to improve the VLA. The KL penalty keeps updates close to the demo distribution.

Why it works: The world model provides cheap rollouts so RL doesn't need expensive real trials; the KL penalty prevents distribution shift. The policy discovers better strategies than the demos because it has a reward signal, but stays conservative enough to remain stable. A handful of real trials for world-model grounding enables significant improvement.

FDPP.narr: Improving a diffusion policy requires either labeled reward data (expensive) or real-world trial-and-error (risky). Learning rewards from pairwise preference annotations — humans rank trajectory pairs — provides a rich signal for fine-tuning without full-trajectory labels, making post-training efficient and practical.
FDPP.how:
The problem: Reward learning for RL typically requires labeling every trajectory; pairwise comparisons are easier for humans but extracting a scalar reward from preferences is statistically expensive and unstable.

The mechanism: Collect trajectory pairs from a pretrained diffusion policy and ask annotators to rank them ("A is better than B"). Train a preference model (Bradley-Terry or similar) that assigns a scalar reward to each trajectory. Use this learned reward with RL algorithms (PPO, DPG) to fine-tune the pretrained policy, with KL regularization keeping updates close to the original.

Why it works: Pairwise preferences are natural for humans to provide; Bradley-Terry reward models extract consistent scalar rewards from partial rankings. The pretrained policy provides a strong prior, so RL needs far fewer preference annotations than training a reward model from scratch. KL regularization ensures the policy stays safe and sample-efficient.

Diffusion Meets DAgger.narr: Imitation learning policies fail on out-of-distribution states they never saw in training; classical DAgger queries an expert for correction but requires a real expert on standby. Diffusion-augmented DAgger synthesizes realistic out-of-distribution states by denoising from the policy's mistakes, so the system can query a simulator or learned expert without a human in the loop.
Diffusion Meets DAgger.how:
The problem: DAgger needs an expert available to label newly-encountered states; this is expensive for real robots. States the policy has never seen it may fail catastrophically, creating a compounding error problem.

The mechanism: During training, whenever the policy makes a mistake on a test trajectory, denoise from the error signal to synthesize a realistic observation in that failure mode. Add this synthetic observation to the dataset and query the expert (simulator or learned model) for the correct action. Retrain the policy on the expanded dataset. Repeat: the diffusion process generates diverse out-of-distribution states, and the expert labels them.

Why it works: Diffusion synthesis produces realistic OOD examples instead of random noise; the expert provides ground-truth actions for those states. The policy iteratively covers more of the state space without requiring a real expert for every failure, achieving data-efficient improvement through synthetic-then-expert-label cycles.

Chain-of-Imagination.narr: Long-horizon robotic tasks like "make a sandwich" break when a single diffusion policy tries to predict the entire trajectory; errors compound over dozens of steps. Multi-step visual imagination — an MLLM + diffusion jointly generate intermediate visual sub-goals, then an action policy executes toward those goals — decomposes the task hierarchically without explicit sub-goal annotation.
Chain-of-Imagination.how:
The problem: One flat diffusion policy over a long horizon (e.g., 100+ steps for multi-stage manipulation) accumulates drift and loses the thread of the task; chunking helps but doesn't address conceptual structure.

The mechanism: Use a multimodal LLM (e.g., GPT-4V) to read the task instruction and current image, then generate text descriptions of intermediate visual sub-goals ("bread on plate," "butter applied"). Pass these descriptions to a diffusion model to generate imagined future observations (visual frames). Use an action policy to generate the next action toward the first imagined sub-goal. Execute, replan when close, repeat.

Why it works: The MLLM breaks the long task into conceptual milestones; diffusion synthesizes realistic images for those milestones, grounding the plan in visual space. The action policy only needs to solve short-horizon primitives to reach each imagined goal. This hierarchical imagination-then-execution structure naturally handles long, multi-step tasks without explicit reward engineering.
